module.name: Provisioner
module.changelog: *1.3.0* Getting started. A new profile can be made from the module's library (Start From, on a new profile): Polycom VVX, AudioCodes 420HD, Grandstream GRP and WebKit, and entries marked (untested) for Cisco SPA, Fanvil X, Mitel 6800 and Yealink T, each copied in with its resources and yours to edit from then on; a file the library cannot ship, such as firmware, is made with nothing uploaded and says what to upload. A new setting, Provisioning Server (ORYK_PROVISIONING_SERVER), is {{provisioning.server}} in a template; blank is the Hostname followed by /provisioner. Notices over the section bar say what to do next on a PBX that is just starting -- add a first profile, a first user, a first client -- on the module's pages only, never the dashboard. One goes by itself once it no longer applies, its button leads to where the thing is done, and its x dismisses it for every admin; Settings -> Show Dismissed Notices Again brings them back. A client's Device offers -- Auto Create --: saving makes a PJSIP device on the next free 999... number, with no extension and no user, and puts the client on it. The class behind the two dashboard warnings is renamed DashboardNotices. *1.2.9* A user's Services tab is two lists, Service Packs and Services, and nothing is saved as a box is ticked: a changed row is marked, and Save in the action bar asks first with what will be assigned and unassigned, what the user gains and loses, and what it keeps through another pack; Reset puts the boxes back. Everything saved at once is one change and at most one job, so swapping one pack for another no longer revokes and grants again what both give. A pack opens to show everything it gives, and a click on the line above that list shows it as a tree; a service held through a pack has a half-filled box. Jobs gain the reason Changed, for several services saved at once. Services have an owner: the module's own (0) are deleted and written again from its defaults on every install or upgrade, keeping their assignments, and a default a release drops goes with its links and assignments; a service made on the Services page is never touched; a default whose slug a release changes is carried to the new one, and install names any it removes. The question before a save says what a gain or loss does on the PBX. The Services list's Assignments column is now Holders: it counts, and opens, everyone who has the service, through a pack included. A failed service has Retry beside it on the user's Services tab. A job records which administrator made it. Every command that changes something is answered only to a POST *1.2.8* Services now do something. Assigning or unassigning one, deleting one, or putting a service into a pack or taking it out writes a job for every user whose services that changes, and starts it at once: one step for each service the user gains or loses -- the service itself and each one under it -- and none for a service the user still has another way. A user's jobs run one at a time, in order; different users' side by side. Each step runs the module's own reaction first and then every module that hooks it: other modules declare serviceGranted and serviceRevoked hooks on Oryk_provisioner in their module.xml (docs/hooks.md), every service or, with a services attribute on the method, only the ones it names. The module's own: Voicemail makes or takes away the user's mailbox (the messages are kept), Call Recording forces recording of the user's calls or puts it back to Don't Care, On Demand Recording enables or disables it, Find Me Follow switches Find Me/Follow Me on or off. A step that throws stops that job for that user only; the user's next job runs, the failed one is tried again after it, and with nothing left it waits for Retry. A new Jobs section (with Logs, Bans and Overview) lists them, filtered by state, reason and source in the address, and each has a page with its steps; the dropdowns gain Jobs; a user's Services tab says which services are queued, running or failed; Overview lists a user's jobs. Saving or deleting a service that changes users' services says how many first. A user deleted anywhere in FreePBX loses its assignments and jobs. An upgrade that regroups the module's own services queues jobs for the users that changes, run by a new minute job. When the last job has run and FreePBX has Apply Config raised, the worker runs fwconsole reload once -- which applies anything else pending too. Finished jobs are kept 30 days *1.2.7* A new Services section, beside Users, Clients and Profiles. A service is a name, and can be put under any number of other services and have any number under it, so one is shared rather than copied: Voicemail under both Basic User and Advanced User. A service with at least one under it is a service pack; nothing is set to make it one, and a service can never be put under itself or anything beneath it. Each service has a slug (call-recording), made from its name and not editable: it is the service's page address (?service=), and renaming a service carries the new slug to everything that referred to the old one. The module brings its own services -- Advanced User, Basic User, Guest User, Call Recording, Find Me Follow, On Demand Recording, Support and Voicemail, grouped into packs -- written on install and upgrade; they cannot be edited or deleted, but a service of your own can be put under or over one. The Services list has two filters, kept in the address: Available, Custom or Module, and All, Services or Packs, each with a count; and an Assignments column. A user's page gains a Services tab: tick a service to assign it, saved as it is ticked, with no Save and no Apply Config. Assigning a pack gives the user every service under it, marked included in the pack. Renumbering a user keeps its services, deleting it removes them, and deleting a service takes it off every user. The row of dropdowns gains Services, listing what the users in view are assigned themselves, with a Pack badge on a pack; on a service, the other dropdowns narrow to the users assigned it. No dropdown picks a row any more just because it is the only one in scope. Templates gain {{extension.services}}: the user's services as slugs joined by commas, those that come through a pack included. Nothing else a phone is served depends on a service *1.2.6* Open provisioning rebuilds the extension and device of a login that still works but has lost them, on its own number and in the lobby, instead of answering 409. A user's clients are the ones on any device of its extension, not only the device numbered like it, and deleting a user deletes every device on its extension. The Users tab lists extensions rather than devices: an extension whose device has been deleted stays on it, marked no device, with its page, its Overview and its Delete, and Save gives it a device back. Promote is gone from a lobby user's page: a user's context is changed in Extensions. After moving one out of the lobby there, Save it once on its Users page to take the transfer guard off, and allow its UCP login in User Manager. A new Overview section lists everything tied to one user or one client -- its clients, provisioning log entries, stored phone logs, and the bans naming it or applying to it, and for a user its User Manager account, mailbox and call history -- so it can be cleaned up from one page. Pick the user or client from the dropdowns and the page reloads on it; from a user's or client's own page the section bar's Overview opens on that row. Each part can be removed where it is listed -- a user's call history included, with Clear Call History, and its voicemail messages, with Clear Voicemail, both of which keep the user -- and Delete All in the action bar removes the user or client with everything listed, after saying how much that is: for a user the whole of a user delete plus the bans naming its extension or its clients' MACs, which a plain delete leaves. Bans that only apply through an address or a profile are marked Keeps and left. On the Users list a Overview button opens Overview on that user, in place of the trash can *1.2.5* Open provisioning is fenced in. Every user it creates is put in the lobby (Settings -> Sign-up Context, ORYK_OPEN_CONTEXT), a context the module writes on Apply Config: extensions, conferences, voicemail and the outbound routes marked Emergency, and nothing else -- no other route, ring group, queue, paging or feature code -- with a call to a lobby phone that it forwards followed in the lobby, no transfer, one call at a time (Lobby Calls), one registered phone per login, no UCP login, and the Lobby Emergency Caller ID. An Allow ban never takes a sign-up out of it. A new username may not be one of a fixed list of reserved names (admin, support, reception and the like, also before an @) or an address at the PBX's own domain: a 400. Sign-ups are limited per address -- an IPv6 /64 -- to 1 a minute and 5 a day (Sign-ups per Minute, per Day), and optionally per PBX (Sign-ups per Day, PBX, which puts a notice on the dashboard when reached): a 429 with Retry-After. An Allow ban on the address lifts the limits. Every sign-up and every refused one is written to FreePBX's security log, worded so its fail2ban jail does not ban for them. Nothing in the module reloads any more: saving or deleting a user raises Apply Config, as Core's Extensions page does, and a sign-up no longer stalls admin saves. A sign-up registers before Apply Config through a Realtime bridge, which install sets up in extconfig.conf and sorcery.conf -- restart Asterisk once -- and a new minute job clears once applied. The Users tab gains Context and Last Seen columns and a Lobby filter, a lobby user's page a Promote button (from-internal, UCP back to its groups), and with Settings -> Lobby Expiry an Expired filter with Delete listed. Users created by open provisioning before this version stay in from-internal: review them -- they are the users whose client is on an internal 02... MAC *1.2.4* Security fixes. The admin tables escape quotes, so a User-Agent or name can no longer inject script into the Logs and Profiles tabs. The module is no longer open to every administrator: one limited to other modules in Admin -> Administrators can no longer use it. Render opens a client's resource as plain text in a new tab instead of a window on the page, and nothing the provisioning endpoint or Render serves can run as a page (nosniff and a sandboxing CSP). A log a phone PUTs keeps its newest 1 MiB, from a whole line; a body over 16 MiB is refused with a 413. Open provisioning makes a new user only for a username of letters, digits, . _ @ and -, up to 64 characters, not only digits and not an IP address; anything else is a 400, and existing logins are unaffected. A username that is an email no longer becomes the account's email, so open provisioning sends no welcome emails. A refused request's body is a bare Forbidden; which ban refused it is on the Logs tab only. Saving a user and open-provisioning sign-ups take a lock, so two at once can no longer be given the same extension. Bans the fail2ban sync imported are deleted 30 days after they expire, and the Bans dropdown lists the newest 100, or only the bans that apply to the row you are on *1.2.3* The row of dropdowns under the section bar gains Logs and Bans, scoped like the others: on a client, user or profile, Logs lists the newest requests from its clients' MACs and Bans every ban that applies to it; on a ban, Users, Clients, Profiles and Logs narrow to what that ban covers. Every provisioning log entry has a page of its own (?log=), opened from the Time column or the Logs dropdown, with Delete and buttons to ban its address or MAC. Each dropdown now says Select, or None when there is nothing to pick, with a chevron beside it; the chosen name is a link to that row and the rest of the box opens the menu. The module's styles move into one stylesheet, assets/oryk_provisioner.css *1.2.2* Bans are the module's own now, kept in a new oryk_provisioner_bans table, and the provisioning endpoint checks them before it answers any request. A ban is Banned (for a number of minutes), Deny (until deleted) or Allow (served in spite of a less specific ban), and names any of an IP address, a MAC address, a user (extension), a client and a profile, matching a request that matches every one it names -- so one ban can allow a user only from one address. When several match, the most specific decides: client, user, MAC, profile, then address, then the one naming more. There is one ban per set of subjects: adding one that names exactly what an existing ban does reopens it. An expired ban stays on the list, greyed, until it is deleted or saved again. A refused request is a 403 on the Logs tab. Every ban counts the requests it decided (Hits), the times it has been in force (Times, with when the current time began), and records what created it (Source, Jail -- editable on its page). Deleting a client or a profile deletes the bans naming it; open provisioning is checked before any user is made; loopback cannot be banned. IP bans sync with fail2ban, both ways, every minute and at once on every save: every address fail2ban bans, in any jail, appears on the Bans tab (Source fail2ban, its Jail, Banned until fail2ban's expiry or Deny when permanent) and expires there when fail2ban lets it go; a ban naming only an IP address is pushed -- Banned into a new banned jail until it expires, Deny into a new deny jail until it is deleted (both every port), Allow onto every jail's ignore list. A ban deleted while fail2ban cannot be reached is finished off by the sync. A ban you made that is in force is never changed by the sync, which never lifts what it did not put there; a fail2ban ban you save on its page becomes yours. Bans on a client, user, MAC or profile stay the provisioner's. fail2ban answers root only, so one setup step as root installs a root-owned helper, one sudo rule and the banned and deny jails: sudo bash /var/www/html/admin/modules/oryk_provisioner/bin/oryk-fail2ban-setup -- run for you by fwconsole as root, and shown under the Bans table until then; on a PBX set up for 1.2 it replaces the helper and sudo rule that version installed. Settings -> Deny After (ORYK_BAN_DENY_AFTER, off by default) turns a Banned ban into a Deny the Nth time it comes into force. The State label on the Bans tab is a menu that changes a ban's state there and then. Settings -> Fail2ban Sync (ORYK_FAIL2BAN_SYNC, on by default) pauses the sync; the 1.2 Fail2ban Bans setting is removed from Advanced Settings on upgrade *1.2.1* Open provisioning: Settings -> Provisioning (ORYK_PROVISIONING: Open, Closed or Disabled; Closed by default). While Open, a request for MAC 000000000000 is answered by its HTTP Basic credentials as a User Manager login -- a username no account holds creates a user with that login, as a blank Extension does in the Users editor -- and served as that user's own client, made on an internal MAC with no profile. It answers any address; a wrong password is written to FreePBX's security log. While Disabled, every request to the provisioning endpoint is refused with a 503. A client with no profile is served the profile named after the vendor its User-Agent names (Polycom, Yealink, Grandstream, ..., WebKit), when one exists. Settings -> Hostname (ORYK_HOSTNAME) is what {{server.host}} renders as, and what a blank From Domain falls back to. Deleting a user from the Users tab now deletes every client pointing at it, with the logs it sent, instead of leaving them with no device *1.2.0* A Bans tab over fail2ban: every banned address in every jail, when it was banned and when it expires, and the client whose Public IP it is. Unban from the row; Add Ban bans one address in one jail for the jail's own bantime, and refuses your own address, loopback and the PBX's own. fail2ban only answers root, so the module reaches it through a root-owned helper and one sudo rule, both installed by sudo bash /var/www/html/admin/modules/oryk_provisioner/bin/oryk-fail2ban-setup -- run as root by fwconsole on install, and shown on the tab with what is missing until it has been run. Settings -> Fail2ban Bans (ORYK_FAIL2BAN, on by default) hides the tab and stops the module asking fail2ban anything *1.1.1* A Settings tab, holding the module's PBX-wide settings -- From Domain first. They are the same settings as Settings -> Advanced Settings -> Oryk Provisioner, so a change in either place shows in both. Save checks every value before writing any and stays on the tab. A new setting is one entry in Settings::definitions(): it is registered on install, drawn on the tab and validated with nothing else written *1.1.0* A Users tab, which takes over from Oryk Connect for Extension/User devices: an extension, its User Manager account, its mailbox and its PJSIP device as one number, created, renamed, renumbered and deleted from one page at &user=. A blank number takes the next free one in the 999… range; a typed one has to be free. Renumbering takes the extension settings, account, mailbox, UCP access, call history and every provisioner client pointed at the user to the new number. Deleting removes the extension, the account, and the call history and recordings for good, and leaves the user's clients in place with no device -- Delete says so before it asks. Each user has a Clients tab of the phones provisioned for it, with an Add Client already pointed at it. Every user's endpoint gets a From Domain, written to pjsip.endpoint_custom_post.conf without touching what other modules keep there: the user's own, or Settings -> Advanced Settings -> Oryk Provisioner -> From Domain, or the PBX hostname when that is a domain name. That setting is the one Oryk Connect registered; installing this version takes it over and keeps its value. Install also adds indexes on devices.id, devices.user and userman_users.email. See the README before removing Oryk Connect: RTSP feeds still need it *1.0.20* A log a phone sends back is kept under the client's id rather than its MAC: ASTLOGDIR/provisioner//, shown on the resource editor when a resource is set to Log. Nothing about what is stored changes -- one directory per client, the resource's own name rendered for that client inside it -- only what the directory is called. The id is what a client is and cannot be edited, so correcting a MAC that was typed wrong no longer strands everything that phone had already sent in a directory nothing points at, and deleting a client now prunes its logs by the same id it is deleted by rather than by a MAC it may no longer have. Directories already on the PBX are named after MACs and are not renamed for you: move each provisioner/ to the id of the client that owns it, or delete the ones you do not want to keep. Templates can also ask for {{client.id}} now *1.0.19* A client no longer has to have a MAC address. Write the row for a phone that has been ordered but not unboxed -- give it its profile, its device and the addresses it will sit at -- and fill the MAC in when the handset is in front of you. A client without one is simply never reached: the endpoint finds a client by the MAC in the path a phone asks with, so nothing arrives for it and it is served nothing until it has one. Its Logs tab stays shut for the same reason -- the log is kept by MAC. Typing something that is not a MAC is still refused, and a MAC that is filled in is still associated once: it is the empty box that is now allowed, not a wrong one. The clients table's mac column becomes nullable on upgrade and existing clients are untouched *1.0.18* A client can be given the two addresses somebody setting a phone up already knows: a Private IP, where the handset is on the local network, and a Public IP, where the site it sits behind is reached from outside. Give a client a private address and its row on the Clients list grows a button that opens that phone's own web interface in a new tab, which is the page you want when a handset needs looking at directly -- the button is drawn only on the rows that have an address, and it opens http:// at the address as stored. Both addresses are searched by the box above the list, so a lease off a router finds the phone it belongs to, and both render into a configuration as {{client.private_ip}} and {{client.public_ip}}. Neither is discovered and nothing in the module connects to either: they are written down on the client, and it is the browser that goes there. An address must be an IPv4 or IPv6 address or the save is refused, since one of them ends up in a link. Existing clients have neither until somebody fills them in *1.0.17* A client records when it was last seen: the last time the endpoint answered it with a 200 -- a file served, a configuration rendered, or a log it PUT received. It is a Last Seen column on the Clients list, showing how long ago that was and the exact moment on hover, and the timestamp itself on the client's own page. Sort the column ascending to find the phones nothing has heard from. A refused request does not count as a sighting -- a client that is switched off, or asking for a file its profile does not serve, is reaching the PBX and getting nothing, and those requests are on the Logs tab as they were. It is kept on the client rather than read out of the provisioning log, so clearing the log leaves it alone. Existing clients read as Never until the next request each one is answered *1.0.16* A profile can be switched off too, by the same switch a client has: the toggle on its row on the Profiles list, or the Status field on its own page. Disabled, every client assigned to it is refused -- its files, and anything of its own served by name -- without one of those clients being changed, so switching it back on serves the whole fleet again exactly as before. Use it to take a profile out of service while its files are being rewritten. A client whose profile is switched off says so in the Profile column of the Clients list and in the profile picker on its own page, since the client itself looks perfectly fine. Either switch asks before it acts, in both directions, since it is one press beside Edit and Delete and the only control on either list that changes a row without opening it. Existing profiles are enabled on upgrade *1.0.15* A client can be switched off. The toggle on its row on the Clients list enables and disables it in place, and the same switch is a Status field on the client's own page. Disabled, every request that client makes is refused -- its profile's files, anything served by name, and any log it tries to PUT -- while the client itself, its token and its profile stay exactly as they were, so switching it back on serves what it was serving before. What it asks for while it is off is still written to the provisioning log, which is usually why it was switched off. Existing clients are enabled on upgrade *1.0.14* A resource has a type: Template, File or Log. It used to be inferred -- an uploaded file meant a file and no file meant a template -- so a resource could not be a file until a file was on it, and could not be a log at all. The type is now the only thing that says which, set on the resource editor, and it decides what a phone asking for that filename gets. Log is the new one and the reason for the rest: a phone PUTs its boot and app logs back when it finishes starting up, and a resource of type Log is what says this profile takes one -- what arrives is written to ASTLOGDIR/provisioner// under the resource's own name rendered for that client, a directory per client, so everything one phone has sent is in one place. Fetching the same URL reads the stored log back, exactly as it arrived and not rendered, so Render on a Log row means the same thing it does on any other. A PUT to anything else is still refused. Existing resources are migrated on upgrade: anything with a file uploaded to it becomes File, everything else Template. Also fixed: a client with a token could fetch a resource whose template column was empty -- an uploaded file, usually -- without presenting the token *1.0.13* The module class is a thin adapter over src/. What was one 3,400-line file is sixteen classes in a namespace of its own -- Clients, Profiles, Resources, Matcher, Previews, Template, Endpoint, Pages, Installer, Schema, FileRepo, Tokens, ProvisioningLog, Freepbx, Mac -- loaded by an autoloader the module registers for itself, since BMO autoloads the module class and nothing else. Every method moved verbatim; not one column changed and nothing behaves differently *1.0.12* A client can be given a token. Type it as -- username:password -- and it is hashed with password_hash() when you save; the Token box holds that hash from then on, so leaving it alone leaves the token alone, typing a new user:password over it replaces it, and emptying it takes it away. A colon is what marks a value as a token still to be hashed. A client that has one must present it: the endpoint asks for HTTP Basic credentials and answers 401 until they verify against the stored hash *1.0.11* A resource can serve an uploaded file instead of a template -- firmware above all. Upload one on the resource and it is served exactly as stored, under the resource's filename; remove it and the resource is the template it was, text and all. There is no type to set: the file is the difference. Files are kept in ASTSPOOLDIR/repo, named after the resource id, and go when the resource or its profile does. serveConfig() is now serve(), and it answers a request with no MAC address in it -- a phone fetching firmware sends none -- from the uploaded files, matched by name across every profile *1.0.10* A provisioning log: one row per request the endpoint answered -- MAC, the file asked for, the status it was answered with and when -- written whether or not a client exists for the MAC. Read it at &tab=logs on the module page, or on a client's own Logs tab, which is narrowed by MAC and so shows what a phone was asking for before anybody wrote its client. Metadata only; the rendered configuration is never stored *1.0.8* A device is a client: the row pairing a MAC with a FreePBX device and a profile is named that everywhere -- &client=, a Clients tab, listClients/saveClient/deleteClient -- so "device" now only ever means the FreePBX device it points at. The table is oryk_provisioner_clients; nothing renames it for you, so rename it before upgrading *1.0.7* A profile no longer holds a template of its own: every file it serves is a resource, the main config included, named .cfg like any other. The profiles table drops its `template` column on upgrade and the text in it is not migrated -- copy anything you still want into a resource first *1.0.6* Adding and editing a device is a page of its own at &device=, the shape a profile already had, rather than a modal on the list *1.0.5* Profile resources: a profile serves the other files a phone asks it for -- -phone.cfg, -directory.xml and the rest -- each a filename and a template of its own, edited on a Resources tab of the profile *1.0.4* Unauthenticated device endpoint at engine/provisioner.php, reached as /provisioner/ through a symlink install() puts in the web root: a phone fetches its config with /provisioner/.cfg or ?mac=, no admin login, by bootstrapping FreePBX directly instead of going through config.php *1.0.3* Rendered configuration at ?display=oryk_provisioner&mac=&config=, with {{ }} placeholders filled in from the device, its extension and the profile *1.0.2* Devices and Profiles: a MAC address is associated with a FreePBX device and a profile, and a profile is a name and a block of configuration text *1.0.1* New
module.description: Provision and manage VoIP endpoints with standardized device configurations for softphones, Yealink, Polycom, Grandstream, and other supported devices. Generate configuration data in JSON, XML, key-value, and device-specific formats.
